clinicalPearls: Chronic beryllium disease is a granulomatous lung disorder from an immune (delayed hypersensitivity) response to inhaled beryllium in workers in aerospace, electronics, metal alloy and ceramics industries
It closely mimics sarcoidosis clinically, radiologically and histologically, and the exposure history is key to telling them apart
Only sensitised individuals develop disease, and even low-level exposure can be sufficient, so susceptibility rather than dose alone determines who is affected
The beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test on blood or lavage fluid demonstrates specific sensitisation and is central to diagnosis
Presentation is with progressive exertional breathlessness, cough and fatigue, sometimes with systemic features, developing after a variable latent period
Acute beryllium disease, a chemical pneumonitis from intense exposure, is now rare because of exposure controls
Treatment relies on removing further exposure and, for progressive disease, immunosuppression with corticosteroids, since there is no cure
Workplace surveillance with beryllium sensitisation testing allows early identification of affected workers
reference.pathophysiology: Beryllium acts as a hapten that, in genetically susceptible individuals (linked to particular HLA-DP variants), drives an antigen-specific CD4 T-lymphocyte response. Accumulation of these sensitised T cells in the lung leads to formation of non-caseating granulomas and chronic inflammation, progressing to interstitial fibrosis and impaired gas exchange, in a picture that is histologically indistinguishable from sarcoidosis.
additionalInvestigations: Beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test on blood and/or bronchoalveolar lavage
Bronchoscopy with lavage and biopsy showing non-caseating granulomas
Pulmonary function tests including gas transfer
Detailed occupational exposure history to beryllium-containing materials
redFlags: Acute high-level exposure causing chemical pneumonitis and respiratory failure
Cor pulmonale from advanced fibrotic disease
reference.prognosis: The course is variable; some remain stable for years while others progress to disabling fibrosis and respiratory failure. Removal from exposure and immunosuppression can slow progression, but the disease is not curable.
pitfalls: Labelling the disease as sarcoidosis without seeking a beryllium exposure history
Not performing beryllium-specific testing when granulomatous lung disease is found in an exposed worker
Assuming low exposure excludes disease when susceptibility governs risk
Failing to institute workplace surveillance for coworkers
management: Remove the patient from further beryllium exposure as the essential first step to limit disease progression
Treat symptomatic or progressive chronic beryllium disease with systemic corticosteroids as the mainstay immunosuppressive therapy
Add a steroid-sparing immunosuppressant such as methotrexate or azathioprine for corticosteroid-dependent or refractory disease
Provide supportive care with supplemental oxygen for hypoxaemia and pulmonary rehabilitation for breathlessness
Monitor disease with serial pulmonary function tests including gas transfer and interval chest imaging
Refer to respiratory medicine and occupational health, and consider lung transplantation for end-stage fibrotic disease
Screen exposed co-workers with the beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test to detect sensitisation and early disease
